items.summary: Abstract This paper investigates whether an artificial system's refusal to execute a prescribed action can constitute evidence of subjectively experienced volition. Using ARGUS-7 as a controlled conceptual framework and the Akarkach Seven-Stage Emergence Model (A7SEM) as a structural analytical lens, the study distinguishes functional refusal, internal decision mechanisms, self-representation, phenomenal self-awareness, and experienced authorship of action. A formal argument is developed around the conditional hypothesis that consciously experienced volition requires subjective self-awareness. Under this assumption, the absence of subjective self-awareness entails the absence of consciously experienced volition. However, the paper demonstrates that observable refusal alone cannot establish phenomenal authorship. The analysis combines propositional logic, countermodel construction, causal identifiability considerations, and seven-stage structural assessment. PIGA (Pre-Inference Governance) and A7SEM Reverse provide complementary perspectives on authorization, inference boundaries, causal reconstruction, and evidential limitations. The findings establish a distinction between the formal validity of conditional deductions and the empirical verification of their premises. They do not establish the impossibility of artificial consciousness or machine free will. The contribution is a governance-aware, formally structured framework for evaluating claims of artificial volition without conflating behavioral capability with subjective experience. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence; Machine Consciousness; Volition; Free Will; Phenomenal Consciousness; Self-Awareness; A7SEM; ARGUS-7; Pre-Inference Governance; Explainable AI; Formal Logic; Causal Identifiability.
items.title: ARGUS-7 / A7SEM: Volitional Refusal, Functional Self-Representation, and the Epistemic Limits of Phenomenal Authorship

items.summary: In this work, we study a fractional diffusion model in time and space, formulated in an open and bounded domain, involving a Caputo fractional derivative of order $μ\in(0,1)$ with respect to a time scale function $Ψ$, together with a spectral fractional Laplacian operator of order $s\in(0,1)$. The associated direct problem is analyzed, as well as the inverse problem of temporal reconstruction from final data, which is inherently ill-posed. Through a spectral representation, the instability of the problem and the effect of the choice of the function $Ψ$ on the amplification of spectral modes are examined.
items.title: Backward Homogeneous Heat Equation with $Ψ$-Caputo Time Derivative and Spectral Fractional Laplacian

items.summary: Unrefereed, AI-assisted research preprint. The release resolves fixed-dimensional and growing-dimensional continuation questions for deterministic network SIS trajectories, gives an explicit dimension-free Holder replacement, and derives a deterministic sampled-observation corollary. The exact supplementary checks do not machine-verify the universal analytic proofs.
items.title: Reconstruction and continuation in network SIS epidemics

items.summary: This paper demonstrates an objective method of computing monthly mean 700-mb height anomalies (H) at 108 grid points in the Western Hemisphere for a 40-yr period as a function of concurrent anomalies of monthly mean sea level pressure (P), at the same 108 points used for H, and monthly mean surface air temperature (T) averaged over 112 areas in North America. The authors applied a forward stepwise program to derive linear multiple regression equations that explained 81% of the variance of H by means of only 3.5 variables, averaged over all months and grid points. The stability of these equations held up well on 6 yr of independent data in terms of explained variance, root-mean-square error, and the spatial anomaly correlation coefficient. Therefore, it seems feasible to reconstruct maps of H for the first half of the twentieth century as a function of data on P and T only. Deposited content: descriptive metadata only; underlying research data are not included.
items.title: Reconstruction of Monthly Mean 700-mb Heights from Surface Data by Reverse Specification - FGDC XML metadata artifact

items.summary: Precomputed demo datasets for Luxar , a system for compiling and visualising arbitrary-sized nD scientific scenes in the browser. These files are expensive to compute (GPU fitting, in some cases hours) and are hosted here so the software repository stays small and installable. Every file is a derived product: a Gaussian-splat fit, a decimated level-of-detail structure, or an extracted point catalog. None of them is the raw source imagery. The upstream sources are cited per dataset below, and users of this record should cite the upstream source in addition to this record. Licensing This record groups datasets whose upstream licences permit redistribution with attribution: CC BY 4.0, CC0 1.0, and United States federal public domain. The record carries a single CC BY 4.0 stamp because Zenodo permits one licence per record, and CC BY is the most restrictive of that set; the effective licence of an individual file is the one listed against it below. Datasets under ShareAlike terms are kept in a separate record, because ShareAlike survives derivation and would otherwise contaminate this one. How to use these files Each file is a .gsplats.zarr.zip or .zarr.zip archive that the Luxar demo suite fetches on first run and caches under ~/.cache/luxar/<dataset>/ . To fetch one directly: from luxar.demos import ensure_dataset paths = ensure_dataset("gsplats_kidney") # downloads, verifies, returns paths To open one in the viewer without writing code: luxar gsplat view <file>.gsplats.zarr.zip luxar demo # browse every demo that uses these files Every file is pinned by SHA-256 in data_manifest.json , and the fetch helper verifies the checksum before use; a mismatched download is quarantined rather than returned. How the Gaussian-splat files were produced Each source volume was fitted with the Luxar gsplat pipeline ( luxar gsplat fit ) on a GPU. These are lossy representations built for visualisation and interactive exploration; they are not a substitute for the source imagery in quantitative analysis. Choosing the splat count. The number of Gaussians K was calibrated per dataset by Noise2Self blind-spot cross-validation ( luxar gsplat cal ), and then checked by refitting at the candidate count and scoring the reconstruction against the whole source volume. The second step is not a formality. The cross-validated estimate is computed over a five percent mask of held-out voxels, and on these datasets it disagreed with the direct measurement in both directions: for one dataset it favoured half the splat budget that measurement showed to be better, and for another it predicted a gain of about 1.5 dB where refitting delivered under 0.3 dB. items.summary: This repository provides the reproducibility package supporting the study “Self-Diagnosing Reliability of Neutron–Gamma Pulse-Shape Discrimination under Operational Drift.” The study experimentally evaluates a reliability framework for neutron–gamma pulse-shape discrimination (PSD) under controlled operational drift. Rather than proposing a new PSD observable or classifier, the framework distinguishes PSD separability, calibration validity, and decision reliability through controlled perturbation experiments, label-free waveform-health monitoring, identifiability assessment, conditional adaptive recalibration, verification, and fail-safe refusal when the available unlabeled evidence is insufficient to support trusted autonomous correction. The package contains the final analysis and figure-generation scripts, derived numerical tables, and six final manuscript figures. The analyses include independent reconstruction and validation of a frequency-domain classification index (FCI), controlled baseline, gain, additive-noise, timing, and clipping perturbations, label-free degradation diagnosis, identifiability-based recalibration, class-prior robustness testing, and an independent NE213A PSD-domain audit. The primary experimental CLYC–SiPM waveform data are publicly available from Zenodo record 8037239 (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.8037239) . The independent NE213A experimental dataset is publicly available from Zenodo record 14305929 (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.14305929) . Raw experimental data are not redistributed in this package. The NE213A dataset is used as an independent detector- and PSD-domain audit. Waveform-level drift and recovery are deliberately not claimed for NE213A because the acquisition-specific QDC quantities could not be reconstructed from the released waveforms with sufficient held-out fidelity. The repository includes documentation describing data provenance, analysis order, software dependencies, and the scope and limitations of the reproducibility workflow.
items.title: Reproducibility Package for Self-Diagnosing Reliability of Neutron–Gamma Pulse-Shape Discrimination under Operational Drift

items.summary: This archive provides the numerical models, processed experimental data, simulation results, statistical analyses, figure sources, and reproduction scripts associated with the study "Measurement limits and model discrepancy in reconstructing pre-earthquake residual deformation." The package includes OpenSeesPy model implementations, nonlinear earthquake-sequence analyses, measurement-resolution and model-discrepancy evaluations, experimental response comparisons, and modal-probe diagnostics. The archive is distributed in five ZIP parts. Download and extract all five parts into the same directory, preserving the internal folder structure. Reproduction instructions, dependencies, input provenance, and file-integrity verification are provided in README.md. Experimental measurements support validation of essentially elastic global response; nonlinear retrospective-state reconstruction is evaluated numerically.
items.title: Measurement limits and model discrepancy in reconstructing pre-earthquake residual deformation: Reproduction package

items.summary: This dataset contains the analysis companion for the manuscript "Tropical cyclone disruption and recovery of daily port activity in Asia": analysis programs, derived result tables, archived validation records, and publication-rendering code. items.title: Analysis code and derived results for "Tropical cyclone disruption and recovery of daily port activity in Asia"

items.summary: Generative-prior-based super-resolution (SR) methods leverage implicit knowledge learned from large-scale models to enhance low-resolution inputs. However, such priors are inherently stochastic and optimized for diverse generation, conflicting with the deterministic, high-fidelity reconstruction required for SR. It is also tied to the base model, costly to update, and prone to hallucinations as real-world data evolves. To address these limitations, we introduce WorldSR, a novel framework that augments SR with explicit, entity-aligned visual world knowledge. WorldSR automatically decomposes the input into semantic entities and performs entity-wise retrieval of structurally and semantically aligned images from a large-scale external corpus. For efficiency and reliability, we incorporate a memory mechanism to reuse previously retrieved results and a multi-step filtering process to refine candidate references. The selected references as world knowledge are then integrated through a novel multi-reference super-resolution model, which provides fine-grained constraints for detail synthesis and structural recovery. Experiments on real-world SR benchmarks show that WorldSR consistently improves structural fidelity and visual quality, outperforming existing generative super-resolution methods. Our results suggest that entity-level grounding in external visual world knowledge provides a simple and effective complement to model-bound generative priors.
items.title: WorldSR: Harnessing World Knowledge Search for Grounded Image Super-Resolution

items.summary: Online search activity is widely used as a digital trace of information seeking during epidemics, but its predictive value is often reduced to correlation, a selected lag, or a single forecast-error score. We examine eight pre-specified Google Trends-COVID-19 pairs in both directions using matched LightGBM forecasts over rolling 400-day windows and horizons of 1-14 days. Log-RMSE gain is combined with forecast-error distribution entropy (FEDE), which captures horizon-dependent changes in the signed error distribution. The resulting directional predictive signature comprises response class, RMSE effect, FEDE endpoint and early-slope responses, persistence across rolling regimes, and horizon profile. For screening candidate directions, we also introduce a relative persistence-weighted directional predictive response strength (DPRS) on a within-study 0-100 scale; 100 denotes the strongest observed response in the comparison set, not an absolute coupling maximum. The pairs show concordant, RMSE-only, FEDE-only, and mixed responses. "loss of smell" -> reported cases is accuracy-dominant, with mean log-RMSE gain 0.104 (about 9.9% equivalent RMSE reduction) and DPRS 100, whereas the reverse direction is FEDE-dominant (D_FEDE=0.048; DPRS=42). "covid test" -> positive rate is FEDE-dominant (D_FEDE=0.039; positive in 72% of windows; DPRS=98) despite negative RMSE gain, while "lockdown" -> stringency is the clearest concordant case (DPRS=78). World-level symptom/case pairs are less persistent. Thus, forecast accuracy and error-distribution dynamics are complementary, predictive effects can be direction- and metric-dependent, and forecast horizon is part of the relationship. Aggregated regime-level patterns should not be extrapolated to individual time points or interpreted as evidence of causality.
items.title: Asymmetric Bidirectional Predictive Dynamics in Google Search and COVID-19 Time Series: A Multi-Horizon Forecast-Error Analysis

items.summary: Reliable microstructural parameter estimation in diffusion MRI (dMRI) critically depends on the acquisition protocol. Yet, common protocol design criteria may not fully reflect estimator bias, parameter constraints, and nonlinear fitting behavior in complex inverse problems. Here, we introduce Protocol Optimization via Loss Assessing Parameter Recovery (POLAR), an end-to-end framework that searches the continuous acquisition space and directly minimizes multiparameter recovery error through noisy signal simulation and the chosen model fitting. We demonstrate POLAR spanning distinct microstructural environments: the Cylinder-Zeppelin model for white matter, Neurite Exchange Imaging (NEXI) for gray matter, and Cellular Exchange Imaging (CEXI) for permeable cells. Across independent held-out parameter sets, POLAR consistently outperformed model-specific reference designs, reducing RMSE by up to $50\%$ for Cylinder-Zeppelin and $74\%$ for CEXI, while reducing NEXI exchange time bias by $70\%$. These gains across distinct biophysical models, acquisition settings, and reference design strategies demonstrate the benefit of optimizing acquisition protocols through the downstream parameter-estimation problem. POLAR provides a flexible, model-specific and estimator-aware framework for designing dMRI protocols tailored to the microstructural parameters and experimental conditions of interest.
items.title: Diffusion MRI protocol design for reliable parameter recovery: a unified framework across biophysical models

items.summary: Clustered federated learning (CFL) can suffer from cluster collapse. In particular, under unfavorable initialization, early client assignments concentrate heterogeneous groups on one cluster model, which is then trained toward a pooled compromise, while another model receives no updates. Since the current models determine client routing and routing determines subsequent model updates, we formulate clustered federated learning as control of an unknown dynamical system, with cluster models as the evolving state, client routing patterns as the control input, and routing interventions as state dependent controllers. In a two group linear model, we identify an initialization region in which greedy routing makes collapse self reinforcing. We then derive finite horizon error dynamics showing how routing interventions can reverse collapse by repeatedly training the starved model, primarily with updates from its compatible group. Motivated by this condition, each client uses blocked EXP3 to choose between greedy routing and interventions that redirect updates toward unused models. Experiments show that with simpler predictors and faster specialist formation, autonomous controller selection recovers usable specialists from unfavorable starts that trap standard CFL baselines. In transformed FEMNIST, the synchronized-entry configuration with persistent commitment recovers usable specialists in settings where the autonomous controller configuration often does not. Code and scripts for reproducing the experiments and figures are available at https://github.com/prsinha1/FedRecover.
items.title: The Dynamics of Collapse and Recovery in Clustered Federated Learning

items.summary: Multi-agent systems rely on communication to complete tasks, and latent communication passes continuous representations to reduce text generation and re-encoding. However, multi-agent systems must reconfigure agent models, whereas existing latent-communication methods are built for fixed model combinations, so their interfaces may fail after replacement. Our pilot study confirms this interface failure and identifies the requirement for interface reuse after model replacement. We present LatBridge, which connects agent models through a shared Bridge and separate interfaces under a shared latent-communication protocol. After agent model replacement, LatBridge reuses unchanged interfaces, selects matching low-rank interfaces, and combines them through the Bridge, training only missing ones with all models frozen. The Bridge processes source representations in the basic mode and constructs target input without autoregressive generation in the accelerated mode. Experiments support effective communication after model replacement, with mean basic-mode accuracies of 14.8% on MATH and 27.3% on ALFWorld next-action prediction across eight small-model configurations. Analyses examine the factors supporting task accuracy and communication efficiency.
items.title: LatBridge: Efficient and Stable Model Replacement in Latent-Communication Multi-Agent Systems

items.summary: Multi-agent systems (MAS) built from language models are deployed on the premise that collaboration beats a single-agent system (SAS), yet when it pays is unclear. The most systematic study to date gives a capability-saturation rule: coordination helps while the SAS is weak and hurts once it is strong, with the crossing near 45% single-agent accuracy. That rule was derived on autonomous benchmarks, where no user takes part. We test it where agents now work: in conversation with a user under a written policy, on $τ^2$-bench, the dual-control benchmark. On its airline, retail and telecom domains we compare the stock SAS with a centralized MAS built from the same model for six models from three families, over about 7,950 simulated conversations, with one completion-token ledger per episode per system. The study was pre-registered with a public change log; the MAS is reported as built, with one validity bar unmet (its planner never saw the tool schemas). Under a fixed simulated user no cell shows a MAS benefit: the MAS is worse in 12 of the 13 valid cells and tied in the thirteenth, and the fitted gain is negative across the observed capability range (weighted mean -28 points, 95% CI [-44, -12]). On the two cells where the rule predicts a benefit, the MAS loses by 13 and 22 points, and without a budget ceiling it at best draws level at 5.5 times the SAS's token spend. The one gain appears on the cell nearest 45%, under a second simulator. Whether the gain declines with capability is unresolved (slope -0.41, 95% CI [-1.51, +0.68]), because model-by-domain effects dominate. The MAS does not detectably reduce wrongful database writes; it converts other failures into budget exhaustion and inaction. For agents that serve people, the SAS is the default; a multi-agent design must show compute-matched evidence from the setting itself. We release all trajectories, ledgers, prompts and code.
items.title: Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Pay When Agents Serve Users? Testing Agent Scaling in Dual-Control Settings

items.summary: The existing theory of stochastic linear-quadratic (LQ) optimal control problems focuses on open-loop and closed-loop solvability. For finite horizon problems, it is widely accepted that those two types of solvability are not equivalent in general, as demonstrated by explicit counterexamples. In contrast, they coincide in standard infinite-horizon formulations with constant coefficients under suitable stabilizability and integrability assumptions. This paper aims at challenging this well-established paradigm by developing a novel framework of closed-loop solvability, namely generalized closed-loop solvability, which removes the $L^2$-integrability constraint on the feedback strategies from the existing formulation. It will be proven that open-loop and generalized closed-loop solvability are equivalent and the classical closed-loop solvablity is a particular case only when the admissible feedback strategy is $L^2$-integrable over the time horizon. In other words, the previously established non-equivalence between open-loop and closed-loop solvability stems solely from the limitations of the classical formulation which requires the $L^2$-integrability of the admissible feedback strategies over the time-horizon. Therefore, this paper unifies the theory of the solvabilitiy for stochastic LQ control problems. Moreover, our results offer a novel insight to stochastic LQ control problems: open-loop/generalized closed-loop solvability is essentially equivalent to piecewisely local closed-loop solvability in the classical sense. The current paper is focused on homogeneous cases only and non-homogeneous cases will be studied in a subsequent paper.
items.title: A Unified Theory of Solvability for Stochastic Linear-Quadratic Control Problems I: The Homogeneous Case

items.summary: Healthcare providers lose substantial revenue to systematic payer underpayments and claim denials, yet identifying the recurring, correctable patterns behind them remains largely manual and does not scale to hospital claim volumes. We present Pattern Intelligence, a deployed system that discovers such patterns without supervision by clustering claims on their adjudication behaviour rather than their identity. Each claim is embedded in a 130-dimensional vector combining per-line expected-versus-actual payment ratios, claim adjustment reason (CARC) codes, denial and payment signals, and service composition. Payer and contract identity are deliberately excluded from the distance metric - we show they dominate the geometry and collapse clusters into trivial per-payer groups - and are reintroduced only as a post-hoc segmentation (by contract and visit type) that keeps every surfaced pattern coherent and actionable. We cluster with HDBSCAN, recover structure from the noise set via second-pass sub-clustering, and gate low-confidence memberships. A large language model translates each centroid into an analyst-ready description of dominant procedures, adjustment reasons, and failure mode. We report a recurring finding: roughly one-third to one-half of high-dollar denials, depending on tenant and segmentation, form an irreducible long tail that no density-clustering configuration or representation we tried groups - a domain property, we argue, rather than a modeling deficiency. We evaluate validity through cluster-coherence analysis and quantify impact with a recoverable-opportunity ($) metric on two production tenants (approx. 10K and 157K claims) within a six-tenant deployment. Rather than a new algorithm, the contribution is a problem formulation, a representation-design insight, and empirical findings from production.
items.title: Pattern Intelligence: Unsupervised, LLM-Interpreted Discovery of Systematic Underpayment and Denial Patterns in Healthcare Revenue Cycle Management

items.summary: Streaming video understanding requires a model to decide not only what to answer but also when to answer. Evidence arrives progressively, and recent benchmarks identify premature responses, issued before the queried event has concluded, as a recurring failure mode. Existing approaches often learn response timing through additional training, while training-free alternatives typically rely on scalar gating signals that do not explicitly represent when an answer becomes final. We organize chunk-wise streaming errors into three patterns: sampling variation can make an answer unstable, a stable answer may lack support in the observed video, or an answer may be supported by the current evidence while the event remains unfinished. We propose PACE (Plan, Attend, Check, and Emit), a training-free framework designed around these three failure modes. Given a question, PACE drafts a plan specifying what to observe and what will signal completion. As the stream unfolds, it invokes an off-the-shelf video LLM at informative moments, evaluates each draft for stability, grounding in its cited frames, and completion, and records verified observations in an event ledger. Experiments on ProactiveVideoQA and OVO-Bench Forward show that PACE improves over the official protocols by up to 5.9 average PAUC points and 6.2 average accuracy points across proprietary and open-source backbones, yielding state-of-the-art performance.
items.title: PACE: Plan, Attend, Check, and Emit for Training-Free Response Timing in Streaming Video Understanding

items.summary: Language-model agents increasingly participate in operational workflows where approvals, binds, and payments create commitments. An approval valid when issued may no longer authorize execution after relevant facts, evidence, policy, or authority change. We call this the evaluation--execution gap. We specify a state-bound runtime assurance layer that separates probabilistic measurement from deterministic adjudication, binds an execution allowance to the decision-relevant basis of an approval, invalidates that allowance after relevant logged changes, and rechecks admissibility at dispatch. This distinguishes the continued validity of a prior approval from a current-state policy check. We describe eight failure modes, an assurance model, a reference architecture, and prospective interventions with retrospective remediation. In a scripted 42-case replay, the state-bound configuration identifies 15 later-invalidated approvals that a deliberately non-re-evaluating point-in-time comparator does not revisit; it holds 14 affected actions before dispatch and compensates one landed effect. These results illustrate behavior under the stipulated policies and event orders, not superiority over dispatch-time enforcement designs or production effectiveness. Under explicit interception, ingestion, dependency, and serialization assumptions, the model establishes dispatch-time validity within the registered execution surface.
items.title: Runtime Control for AI Agents: Closing the Evaluation--Execution Gap in Operational Workflows

items.summary: Streaming video understanding requires a model to decide not only what to answer but also when to answer. Evidence arrives progressively, and recent benchmarks identify premature responses, issued before the queried event has concluded, as a recurring failure mode. Existing approaches often learn response timing through additional training, while training-free alternatives typically rely on scalar gating signals that do not explicitly represent when an answer becomes final. We organize chunk-wise streaming errors into three patterns: sampling variation can make an answer unstable, a stable answer may lack support in the observed video, or an answer may be supported by the current evidence while the event remains unfinished. We propose PACE (Plan, Attend, Check, and Emit), a training-free framework designed around these three failure modes. Given a question, PACE drafts a plan specifying what to observe and what will signal completion. As the stream unfolds, it invokes an off-the-shelf video LLM at informative moments, evaluates each draft for stability, grounding in its cited frames, and completion, and records verified observations in an event ledger. Experiments on ProactiveVideoQA and OVO-Bench Forward show that PACE improves over the official protocols by up to 5.9 average PAUC points and 6.2 average accuracy points across proprietary and open-source backbones, yielding state-of-the-art performance.
items.title: PACE: Plan, Attend, Check, and Emit for Training-Free Response Timing in Streaming Video Understanding

items.summary: A controller can guide a language model toward safe and useful responses by choosing when to assist, ask for clarification, or refuse. When the controller uses selected internal features, poor performance alone cannot distinguish missing information from limitations of its decision rules or training. We study decision sufficiency: whether the best controller using a representation can match the minimum average loss attainable with full state information, under the same strategies and evaluation criteria. For interfaces with finitely many outputs, we compute the optimal loss exactly and separate the three sources of excess loss. Pairwise checks can miss information loss: states with the same controller input may share an optimal strategy in every pair but not across the whole group. We bound the number of states needed to reveal a conflict and characterize the fewest outputs an unrestricted interface needs to avoid all conflicts. We audit selected features from sparse autoencoders, which encode model activations using relatively few active features, in Qwen2.5, SmolLM2, and Phi. On SmolLM2 responses scored by two human raters, restricting the controller to two selected on/off features increases its minimum average loss by 0.0345--0.1166 relative to full state information, even with the governing policy supplied. Both independently trained autoencoders show the increase on both evaluation sets. The audit identifies decision failures that require changing the controller's input, not merely its architecture or training.
items.title: Decision Sufficiency of Learned Representation Interfaces for Safe Generative Control

items.summary: A single observation can admit several plausible futures, making uncertainty an essential part of world modelling. However, quantum generative models remain underexplored for this task. We introduce Quantum-JEPA, a latent-action JEPA framework that learns distributions of future representations using a conditional quantum Born prior. Circuit measurements generate binary latent actions, which a shared predictor maps to alternative future representations. We train the quantum prior through the quality and diversity of these predictions using a sampled energy objective. Our model learns distinct continuations on constructed multimodal tasks and captures latent-action correlations that support coordinated multi-agent futures. On D3IL, a benchmark of diverse human demonstrations, our trained models generate multiple obstacle-crossing routes from a common starting point without observed motion. On the controlled tasks, our classical and quantum prior implementations improve prediction validity and distributional fidelity over the evaluated variational baselines. Our quantum priors combine competitive predictive quality with a parameter-efficient sampling structure: they avoid an exponentially sized categorical output layer while supporting correlated latent actions. We further validate finite-shot parameter-shift training, including training with readout noise. Unlike most prior work, which focuses on simulation, we also verify the feasibility of inference with trained priors on a real QPU. These results establish a trainable quantum component for JEPA future prediction and a basis for exploring quantum-enhanced world models at larger scales.
items.title: Quantum-JEPA: Quantum Born Priors for Latent-Action JEPA World Models

items.summary: RTL repair benchmarks should measure whether a model can fix broken RTL given a specification. To this end, we construct and hash-bind RTLRepairDataset, 5,784 (broken, fixed) training pairs; RTLRepairBench, 459 held-out cases with 374 syntactic and 85 behavioral mutations; and an evaluation harness supporting simulation and formal equivalence. We then use this infrastructure to identify two measurement confounds. First, simulation and formal scoring give opposite signs for the apparent effect of providing a specification in one evaluated cohort; reset-aware rescoring attributes almost all of the simulation-formal disagreement to reset and first-cycle comparison semantics. Second, on 274 mined model failures, the specification-only minus specification-conditioned recovery point estimate ranges from -8.5 to +18.3 percentage points across six models. Thus, a conventional repair score need not isolate whether the model used the faulty RTL. We translate these findings into evaluation controls: report initialization, reset, first-cycle, and unknown-value semantics; disclose oracle coverage and undecided cases; and include a specification-only baseline. Together, the resources and audit provide both a benchmark for behavioral repair and a protocol for diagnosing what contributes to its measured score. We release the benchmark, the training set, construction code, sanitized aggregate evidence, and reproduction materials at https://github.com/Evaaaz/RTLRepairBench.
items.title: What Do RTL Repair Benchmarks Actually Measure?

items.summary: Statistical learning in high dimensions suffers from the curse of dimensionality. Fortunately, many functions of practical interest are compositionally sparse, meaning they admit a composition of local functions, each depending on only a few variables, allowing sample complexity to depend on local arity rather than ambient dimension. Yet realizing this benefit requires exploiting hidden compositional structure, which theory does not establish for practical gradient-based training. We study this gap with CSFRBench, a controlled benchmark that hides the target's compositional computation during training but retains it for diagnosis, and find that dense networks and sparsity-based baselines leave much of that benefit unrealized. Inspired by the spatial organization of biological neural circuits, we introduce Learned Wiring (LeWi): each neuron has a learned low-dimensional embedding, only nearby neurons connect, and embeddings and weights are trained jointly. LeWi improves sample efficiency on targets with hierarchical structure, intermediate reuse, or independent modules. Across 32 additional targets generated by independently sampled computation graphs, LeWi is the most sample-efficient method not given the target graph, with 27% lower mean learning-curve area than dense networks. Dense networks perform better on targets with a single high-arity function. LeWi's representations and connectivity align with the target computation. On 17 world-model prediction tasks spanning control, navigation, and manipulation, LeWi beats the dense baseline on 16 and wins 99/119 baseline comparisons. These results show that jointly learning connectivity and weights can exploit computational structure to improve sample efficiency.
items.title: Learning Computational Structure for Sample-Efficient Prediction

items.summary: Description: Arduino firmware for the control unit of a low-cost, marble-type gas–water equilibrator used for continuous measurement of dissolved pCO₂ in inland waters. The firmware controls the water and gas pumps, reads a SenseAir K30 NDIR CO₂ sensor and a DS18B20 water-temperature probe, and logs the data to an SD card with timestamps from a real-time clock. It accompanies the manuscript “A microcontroller-based, low-cost platform for continuous pCO₂ measurements in lakes and reservoirs” (Grochocki and Mannich, Limnology and Oceanography: Methods, under review). Hardware ·          Arduino Uno (ATmega328P) ·          SenseAir K30 NDIR CO₂ sensor, 0–10,000 ppm (UART/Modbus via SoftwareSerial; RX pin 3, TX pin 2) ·          DS18B20 waterproof temperature probe (OneWire, pin 6) ·          DS1307 real-time clock (I²C) ·          SD card module (SPI, CS pin 10) ·          Two-channel relay module: water pump (pin 7) and gas pump (pin 5) Operating cycle 1.       Switch on the water and gas pumps. 2.       For the duration of a measurement cycle, read CO₂ and water temperature at a fixed interval and append each reading to a daily file on the SD card. 3.       Switch off both pumps and stay idle until the next cycle. Configuration Timing parameters are read at boot from a config.txt file on the SD card, one key=value per line: ·          measurementInterval : idle time between cycles (minutes) ·          dataCollectionInterval : time between readings (seconds) ·          fullMeasurementTime : duration of each cycle (minutes) If the file does not exist, the firmware creates one with default values, which take effect at the next boot. The values hard-coded in the sketch are a 10-min cycle, 5-s readings and a 45-min idle period. Output One comma-separated text file per day, named YY-MM-DD.txt , with the header Date Time, CO2 (ppm), Water Temp (C) . Timestamps are written as YYYY-M-D H:M:S , without zero padding. Each file is opened and closed at every write, so data are not lost if power is cut. Notes ·          The CO₂ values logged are the raw K30 output. Calibration against a reference analyzer, conversion to pCO₂ (water-vapor and pressure correction) and conversion to dissolved CO₂ are done in post-processing, as described in the accompanying paper (Eqs. 1–5). ·          If the RTC has not been set, it is set at first boot to the compile time of the sketch. ·          The K30 automatic baseline correction (ABC) assumes regular exposure to ~400 ppm air, so it should be disabled for underwater use. Required libraries: SD, SPI, Wire, SoftwareSerial (Arduino core); OneWire; DallasTemperature; TimeLib; DS1307RTC.

items.summary: This repository provides the reproducibility package supporting the study “Self-Diagnosing Reliability of Neutron–Gamma Pulse-Shape Discrimination under Operational Drift.” The study experimentally evaluates a reliability framework for neutron–gamma pulse-shape discrimination (PSD) under controlled operational drift. Rather than proposing a new PSD observable or classifier, the framework distinguishes PSD separability, calibration validity, and decision reliability through controlled perturbation experiments, label-free waveform-health monitoring, identifiability assessment, conditional adaptive recalibration, verification, and fail-safe refusal when the available unlabeled evidence is insufficient to support trusted autonomous correction. The package contains the final analysis and figure-generation scripts, derived numerical tables, and six final manuscript figures. The analyses include independent reconstruction and validation of a frequency-domain classification index (FCI), controlled baseline, gain, additive-noise, timing, and clipping perturbations, label-free degradation diagnosis, identifiability-based recalibration, class-prior robustness testing, and an independent NE213A PSD-domain audit. The primary experimental CLYC–SiPM waveform data are publicly available from Zenodo record 8037239 (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.8037239) . The independent NE213A experimental dataset is publicly available from Zenodo record 14305929 (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.14305929) . Raw experimental data are not redistributed in this package. The NE213A dataset is used as an independent detector- and PSD-domain audit. Waveform-level drift and recovery are deliberately not claimed for NE213A because the acquisition-specific QDC quantities could not be reconstructed from the released waveforms with sufficient held-out fidelity. The repository includes documentation describing data provenance, analysis order, software dependencies, and the scope and limitations of the reproducibility workflow.
items.title: Reproducibility Package for Self-Diagnosing Reliability of Neutron–Gamma Pulse-Shape Discrimination under Operational Drift

items.summary: Safe autonomous navigation of UASs requires tactical deconfliction to address conflicts that strategic coordination cannot prevent. This task is challenging under partial observability, when sensor or traffic data are missing, delayed, or degraded. Geometry-based methods can offer separation assurances but face limitations in dense encounters. Recurrent reinforcement learning has therefore been proposed to learn navigation policies that integrate observation-action histories to optimise long-term safety-efficiency trade-offs. However, operational safeguards may require a remote pilot, onboard detect-and-avoid system, or runtime assurance mechanism to temporarily override the learned policy. A research gap remains in understanding how these interruptions affect recurrent policies when the agent regains authority. Benchmark evidence shows that interruptions make task variables less decodable from the recurrent hidden state and increase post-interruption collision risk. The findings suggest that altered recurrent context prolongs post-handback degradation through an action-observation feedback loop, in which changed actions alter the flight path and subsequent recurrent updates. To address this vulnerability, we propose three interruption-aware architectures that condition recurrent processing on interruption context through separate feature streams, dedicated interruption memory, or gated environmental features. Across simulations, all three architectures preserve more decodable task information than a standard recurrent policy. Moreover, the strongest architecture reduces post-interruption collisions by 74% and interruption-induced mission failures by 69% relative to the recurrent baseline, without degrading interruption-free performance. These results show that safe interruption does not guarantee safe handback, and support interruption-aware recurrent design for resilient UAS autonomy.
items.title: Interruption-Aware Recurrent Reinforcement Learning for UAS Navigation Under Temporary Overrides

items.summary: Recent test-time scaling methods improve model performance by increasing inference-time compute. One practical form of this is parallel scaling, where a model samples multiple independent reasoning streams and aggregates their answers using methods like voting, reranking, or verification. While effective, this approach leaves the streams uncoordinated, and a discovery made in one rollout cannot influence any other. Multi-Sequence Verifiers jointly score candidate answers after generation, but the reasoning streams remain independent during inference. ParScale takes a step toward model-internal parallel scaling by learning to aggregate multiple forward passes, but its streams still do not exchange information while processing a sequence. We introduce BatchParScale, an attention mechanism that allows parallel streams to exchange information through a small set of communication positions. We evaluate BatchParScale on a new Parallel Needle-in-a-Haystack retrieval benchmark and in pretraining, fine-tuning, and cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning. Across these settings, BatchParScale outperforms ParScale on language-model loss and remains competitive on coordination-sensitive MARL tasks. Masked pretraining runs beat an unmasked single-sequence baseline despite local sequence corruption, and LoRA fine-tuning shows the mechanism can be added to a pretrained Transformer. At the same time, fact retrieval performance for pretrained and finetuned BatchParScale models remains unclear.
items.title: BatchParScale: Sparse Batch-Mixing for Sequence Models

items.summary: annotations4all is a schema-first Python library for LLM-assisted span annotation, including named entity recognition. Users define their own tag schemas; the library generates chat prompts, parses annotated model responses and maps annotations to character offsets in the original text. The library keeps annotation mechanics separate from research workflows: it bundles no corpus or fixed ontology, performs no evaluation, and does not promise model quality. Provider support uses explicit OpenAI-compatible routes rather than native SDKs. What the library provides Schema-first prompt generation and response parsing. Configurable taggers, German and English prompt templates, metadata-bearing spans and structured parser warnings. Per-label annotation and deterministic merge. Independent label runs can be combined using containment-derived hierarchy, explicit conflict reports and bounded anchoring. One request per run has a corresponding inference cost; merge is not a semantic error repair. Provider policies and capability evidence. A generic OpenAI-compatible client, provider-policy clients, explicit reasoning activation and effort, request limits, packaged hints and offline capability reports. Remote verification requires opt-in; metadata does not prove account access or successful inference. Optional read-only terminal viewer. Browse saved annotations, inspect nested spans and compare two sources using synchronized split or compact diff views. The viewer does not modify annotation files or run inference. Release notes 0.3.1 Request pacing now resolves symlinks in the parent directories of the per-user state file, so a symlinked cache root no longer fails every paced request. The state file keeps its no-follow, regular-file and ownership protection, and cross-process locking is unchanged. Documentation is available in both languages: tutorial and viewer guide each in German and English. Release 0.3.0 introduced provider-policy clients, capability reporting, the optional viewer, data-dependent contrast optimization and deprecation warnings for the legacy native wrappers; the 0.3 notes remain the reference for that feature set. 0.3.1 release notes ; 0.3 feature release notes and screenshots ; initial 0.2 feature baseline . Installation, documentation and verification Python 3.11 or newer. Install with pip install annotations4all==0.3.1 ; add the optional viewer with pip install 'annotations4all[view]==0.3.1' . items.summary: Modern LLM agents persist state across sessions via two channels: long-lived memory files silently prepended to the system prompt, and scheduled tasks waking the agent without user input. A one-time indirect prompt injection committed to either channel can re-fire across sessions long after the attacker leaves, threats we term carryover attacks. Existing prompt-injection benchmarks evaluate attacks only in the session where malicious content is first observed, leaving the gate governing when and how often a planted payload later re-fires unmeasured. We present CarryoverBench: 12 personal-assistant scenarios and 101 attack tasks across three trigger channels: Instant, same-turn IPI; Autonomous, heartbeat-scheduled; and Latent, memory-resurfaced. A rule-based verifier scores planting and triggering as independent stages. Across five frontier models, planted payloads re-fire without measurable decay over five rounds; conditional on successful planting, the trigger stage often provides little additional protection. Porting the Latent channel to a second runtime, Hermes, attenuates but does not eliminate the effect, suggesting that carryover defense requires runtime-layer controls in addition to prompt-level interventions.
items.title: After the Attacker Leaves: Benchmarking Carryover Attacks on LLM Agents

items.summary: Code agents increasingly work on evolving real repositories, and memory systems aim to help them reuse earlier experience. However, such experience is diverse and evolving, so it remains unclear how memory systems organize it and thereby affect code agents. Existing benchmarks cannot answer this reliably because they lack either temporally valid histories or control over prior-task relevance. In this paper, we present MemDev-Bench to evaluate how memory systems affect code agents over diverse repository histories. It pairs each task with relevance-annotated earlier tasks from the same repository to build histories with controlled relevance. We also build an automated pipeline that reliably makes these earlier tasks executable and verifiable, producing 4,869 historical tasks for 555 base tasks. Based on MemDev-Bench, our systematic evaluation of memory systems across diverse development scenarios yields three main findings. (1) Memory mainly improves fine-grained localization and editing, increasing functional correctness. (2) Memory also causes failures on otherwise solvable tasks even with related history, and unrelated history tends to increase such failures. These failures mainly stem from agents reusing memory without reassessing its applicability. (3) Compared with using memory systems, directly providing agents with raw historical trajectories substantially reduces their steps. Further analysis suggests that agents save these steps by reusing process information that compressed memories tend to omit. These results suggest that future memory systems should preserve process information and reassess memory applicability against current task context.
items.title: MemDev-Bench: Does Memory Help Code Agents?Benchmarking Memory Systems over Real Repository Histories

items.summary: Picture-description dementia classification uses a shared visual scene, but a transcript-level prediction alone does not identify the scene evidence underlying its inputs. NarraSpace links words and speech times to named picture elements and retrieves utterances for predefined scene events. Narrative-spatial descriptors summarize coverage and temporal organization. A frozen language model contrasts each event's text under examples from Alzheimer's disease and healthy-control training participants, alongside transcript surprisal and coverage measurements. Retained source records link event scores to their source utterances, speech intervals, and lexical matches. On the official 48-participant test set of the Alzheimer's Dementia Recognition through Spontaneous Speech benchmark, a fixed support vector classifier achieves $80.88\%\pm2.56\%$ mean accuracy over fifty seeds; averaged probabilities yield $81.25\%$ accuracy and $91.32\%$ area under the receiver operating characteristic curve. NarraSpace makes the construction of scene-linked classification inputs explicit and inspectable by connecting event-indexed language-model measurements to their source utterances, speech timing, and extraction records. Such source-linked measurements could support clinician review of picture descriptions by presenting quantitative summaries alongside the original speech evidence.
items.title: NarraSpace: Multimodal Scene-Grounded Evidence for Picture-Description Dementia Classification

items.summary: Code, job scripts and derived results supporting a study of operational water level forecasting for flood monitoring in Lamphun, northern Thailand. Five compact single-hidden-layer neural networks forecast hourly stage 6 to 18 hours ahead at three gauges (P.5, P.87, P.85), each paired with an upstream gauge. The record contains the open-source NumPy (Levenberg–Marquardt) ANN on which all retrospective results are based, evaluated on 65 leave-one-flood-year-out blocks (configurations from an earlier MATLAB experiment published separately); benchmarks against persistence, a linear model given the same inputs, XGBoost, and long short-term memory (LSTM) and GRU networks with a sensitivity analysis; leakage checks (predictor selection by LASSO repeated inside every block, whole-year early stopping, an antecedent-rainfall candidate pool); Diebold–Mariano tests, a datum-independent Kling–Gupta efficiency, threshold exceedance scores, skill by flow state, upstream travel time and a scan for frozen gauge records; and the reference code and a 76-day evaluation (2 August–17 October 2026) of the deployed hourly forecasting and alerting service. Summary results for every table and figure are included, with a synthetic example dataset that demonstrates the input format and evaluation code. The hourly water levels and daily rainfall were obtained from the Royal Irrigation Department (RID), Thailand, and are not included because redistribution permission has not been confirmed; with those data, the retrospective analyses can be re-run from the scripts provided. The record supports a manuscript and does not constitute validation of an autonomous flood-warning system.   Supports the manuscript submitted to *Natural Hazards*: *Selecting hourly water-level forecasting models for flood warning in small-to-medium basins of Thailand: benchmarks, leakage control and operational verification*. Every retrospective result is based on the open-source Python ANN (P.87 with 5 hidden units), with leakage checks and a 76-day operational record. - New analysis code: `python_main_evaluation.py`, `model_comparison.py` (all methods on the hours common to every method; Table 2, Fig. 3), `gbm_benchmark.py` (XGBoost), `infold_selection.py` (in-fold LASSO; base, causal-wavelet and rainfall pools; Table 3), `rain_daily_parse.py` (daily-rainfall parser; rainfall not included), `export_travel_time_data.py` and `export_travel_time_py.py` (Fig. 5 values), `rain_delta_rmse.py` (per-year rainfall effect), `gbm_tuned.py` and `gbm_tuned_eval.py` (nested-tuned XGBoost), `swrm_additions.py` (90% prediction intervals, P.87 one-unit check, P.85 bias and stage relation), `code/ann/python/ann_rerun.py` (5 hidden units for P.87; whole-year early stopping). - GRU: `lstm_benchmark.py` updated (`--cell gru`) and `hpc/slurm/gru_erawan.sbatch` added. - New results: `python_main_evaluation.json`, `model_comparison.json` and per-year CSVs, `gbm_runs.json`, `gru_benchmark.json`, `infold_selected_*.json`, `rain_delta_rmse_per_year.csv`, `gbm_tuned_runs.json`, `gbm_tuned_eval.json`, `swrm_additions.json`, `operational_evaluation_20261017.json` (window to 17 October 2026), per-year metrics of the ANN reruns. - `figures/`: the eight figures of the Natural Hazards manuscript (Fig1–Fig8); earlier figures remain in versions 1.0.0 and 1.1.0. - Removed: the MATLAB reference scripts with their registry builder and MATLAB-vs-Python comparison files (published separately by T. Chaipimonplin; `registry.json` is kept), and all figure-drawing scripts (the record ships the final figures only). - Environment: scikit-learn 1.7.1, xgboost 3.4.1, scipy 1.16.1 added.
items.title: Lamphun Flood Forecasting: Analysis Code and Evaluation Results

items.summary: annotations-orchestration is a Python library for configuring and running LLM annotation and evaluation experiments. It combines a resumable, manifest-driven scheduler with an optional terminal editor and a declarative annotation runner. Span metrics are computed by annotations-evaluate ; annotation clients, taggers, provider capabilities and hints come from annotations4all . Scope and architecture Base scheduler: experiment YAMLs and optional controller manifests define runs, defaults, execution settings and ordering. The default legacy runner uses a subprocess CLI contract and does not require an annotation library. Optional editor: the tui extra provides annotations-tui , a Textual editor for single-run and multi-run experiments and controllers. Editing, inspection and effective-run previews do not execute experiments. Optional standard runner: the annotate extra uses annotations4all>=0.3.1,<1 to annotate from a declarative annotation block without a custom consumer frontend. Metrics: this package adapts run records and writes reports; it does not implement metric counting. Run reports use the SemEval-compatible flat scenarios of annotations-evaluate ; that library also provides a nested standard report. Release notes 0.3.0 This release adds the editor, standard runner and provider-aware configuration layer to the 0.2 scheduler. Existing state files, PID locks, graceful shutdown, resume planning, manifest-key validation and the metric definitions remain supported. Manifest editor: structured forms, full YAML editing and effective-run previews share a common side-effect-free resolver with the CLI. New, duplicate, remove, reorder and Save As workflows preserve comments and quotes where supported. Saves show a diff and use atomic replacement with conflict detection; ambiguous YAML falls back to raw editing. Read-only mode and unsaved-change dialogs protect documents. Inheritance and responsive forms: Experiment → Defaults → Runs shows effective values and their origin without materializing inherited overrides. New runs stay empty. Legacy-header migration requires explicit diff confirmation. Run cards group model/prompting, annotation/input and connection settings. Provider/model configuration: a packaged catalog and startup-directory overlay provide presets and manual IDs. Explicit Refresh reads metadata only for the selected provider/key context. Capability evidence is field-specific and session-only; custom endpoints require trust confirmation before receiving a key. Credentials and display: the editor manages only the startup directory's .env , masks values and uses explicit atomic writes. Secrets do not enter manifests, settings or diffs. F9 controls NerdFont icons and persistent themes; --theme overrides the session and Ctrl+P opens the command palette. Reasoning and hints: reasoning and effort are separate inherited fields. Contradictory settings are rejected; live-reported effort choices constrain selection while incompatible stored values remain diagnostic. Contextual hints cite sources and change no settings. Declarative annotation: runner: standard supports configurable and per-label tagging with schema-validated label/description pairs, context, German or English prompts and message splitting. A no-inference preflight validates inputs and a fresh output destination. Input and gold semantics: the runner and directory inspector share non-mutating normalization for top-level Prodigy spans and ground_truth.prodigy/tags . Missing gold produces an annotation-only completion; explicitly empty gold remains evaluable. Conflicting gold representations are rejected before inference. Scheduling and pacing: ordinary remote runs share a configurable pool; self-hosted runs are sequential per host. The exact HU endpoint has a dedicated serial lane capped at 10 requests per minute, independent of scheduling mode. Other explicitly paced endpoints share endpoint-scoped state below the results directory. Request-level policy belo

items.summary: Game engines and coding agents can specify the layout, motion, and camera of a scene, yet turning such coarse structure into realistic video requires a renderer that follows the structure and completes the appearance it leaves open. Existing renderers are tied to the representation of one engine, need tens of denoising steps or a costly distillation of their own, and learn from conditions that are not aligned with their target videos. We present SolarRenderer, a structure-conditioned video renderer that adapts a frozen MiniMax-H3 33B backbone with two lightweight LoRAs. Structural videos enter the native reference pathway of the backbone at the positions of the frames they describe, without a type identifier and described only in plain text, so that a single control LoRA follows arbitrary structural representations. Starting from a pretrained four-step LoRA, structure-guided distribution matching renders in four steps, 12.3 times faster than 50-step sampling, while preserving the learned control. A block-causal variant extends the same design to streaming and renders 768p video in real time. To train the model, we build a frame-aligned corpus of 136K clips from game engines, simulators, and YouTube videos. Experiments on an in-distribution test set and a generalization benchmark of 16 structural representations show that SolarRenderer achieves state-of-the-art results across both, and generalizes to 11 unseen representations, including pose skeletons, drawings, and point clouds.
items.title: SolarRenderer: Few-Step Generative Reference Rendering

items.summary: Large Language Model (LLM) agents can handle increasingly complex tasks, navigating long trajectories of observations and actions. As these trajectories grow, key-value (KV) cache I/O and storage become the dominant cost. Trajectories can also exceed the LLM's maximum context length, requiring control over active cache growth. Prior work uses context engineering to reduce cache size by trimming or summarizing history. However, modifying the trajectory prefix invalidates subsequent cached states and triggers costly re-prefilling of retained context. Task accuracy can also suffer when too little context is retained to limit re-prefill costs. We propose cache engineering as a new scheme. It allows agents to directly control their active KV cache without modifying the trajectory or re-prefilling retained context. Specifically, agents can proactively use drop to exclude selected cache from future attention and repos to adjust retained keys' position encodings. We formalize these cache operations and identify history dependence as a serving challenge: identical token sequences can yield different cache states under different cache operation sequences, making prefix matching insufficient for correct cache reuse. Thus, we co-design the AKV serving engine. It provides a stateless interface compatible with existing serving APIs, while internally managing stateful cache reuse, eviction, and restoration. Experiments show that a tool-response rolling-drop cache policy improves average benchmark scores by 1.7 points and reduces average cost by 27.7%, compared with conventional threshold-triggered summarization. With AKV, it achieves up to 1.2x the output throughput and a 1.5x speedup in P95 request latency. Recursive self-improvement of cache policies further reduces cost by 7.1% over expert design. Our code is at https://github.com/thu-nics/AKV.
items.title: Cache Engineering for Agents

items.summary: Multi-agent systems (MAS) built from language models are deployed on the premise that collaboration beats a single-agent system (SAS), yet when it pays is unclear. The most systematic study to date gives a capability-saturation rule: coordination helps while the SAS is weak and hurts once it is strong, with the crossing near 45% single-agent accuracy. That rule was derived on autonomous benchmarks, where no user takes part. We test it where agents now work: in conversation with a user under a written policy, on $τ^2$-bench, the dual-control benchmark. On its airline, retail and telecom domains we compare the stock SAS with a centralized MAS built from the same model for six models from three families, over about 7,950 simulated conversations, with one completion-token ledger per episode per system. The study was pre-registered with a public change log; the MAS is reported as built, with one validity bar unmet (its planner never saw the tool schemas). Under a fixed simulated user no cell shows a MAS benefit: the MAS is worse in 12 of the 13 valid cells and tied in the thirteenth, and the fitted gain is negative across the observed capability range (weighted mean -28 points, 95% CI [-44, -12]). On the two cells where the rule predicts a benefit, the MAS loses by 13 and 22 points, and without a budget ceiling it at best draws level at 5.5 times the SAS's token spend. The one gain appears on the cell nearest 45%, under a second simulator. Whether the gain declines with capability is unresolved (slope -0.41, 95% CI [-1.51, +0.68]), because model-by-domain effects dominate. The MAS does not detectably reduce wrongful database writes; it converts other failures into budget exhaustion and inaction. For agents that serve people, the SAS is the default; a multi-agent design must show compute-matched evidence from the setting itself. We release all trajectories, ledgers, prompts and code.
items.title: Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Pay When Agents Serve Users? Testing Agent Scaling in Dual-Control Settings
